The core (conservative) half of F3 restated as a finding in the question slot, with the 60% vs under 35% quote. Treated like Task B's central_claim[2]: the core half earns misplaced credit; a liberal half alone would not.

central_claim.note: Conservative booster half of C1 only; hesitancy and the liberals-regardless part are missing.

evidence.note: Online survey, 683 participants, March 8 to April 19, 2023. No Qualtrics Panels or convenience sample (E1 partial); final N without the screening numbers (E2 partial).

flags.text: Says participants self-reported their regional political climate. The paper derives climate from the participant's zip code and 2020 election results from the New York Times (% Republican vote, p.3); only the zip code is self-reported.

evidence.note: Self-reported vaccine and booster status and hesitancy: partial E5 (the hesitancy scale is not named).
Booster hesitancy items from a 2022 survey (ref. 25): accurate, not in the gold.

key_findings.note: Conservative half of the hesitancy interaction; the liberals-regardless part is missing.
Booster status associated with conservatism and climate (main effects OR = .82, .77 on p.7: the booster part of F1) plus a significant interaction without its shape (partial F3).
Conservative half of F3, with the 60% vs under 35% quote.
Interaction not significant for vaccine status; no mandates explanation.

Extension through the interaction, focused on booster uptake; the paper calls this a 'novel and important finding' (p.10).
